theme: Why are times not kept by the Almighty? Bildad’s last word
readingInstruction: Read Job 24:1-26:14. Job begins by asking why God does not set times for judgment, Bildad gives his last, very short speech, and Job answers with a hymn to God’s power. Read chapter 26 as a poem about how little we know.
settingTheScene: This is the third and final cycle of speeches, and you can feel the friends running out of things to say. Eliphaz has spoken already. Bildad has only six verses left in him, and Zophar will not speak at all. Job’s side of the argument keeps growing. In these chapters he first lists injustices that God seems to ignore, and then he turns and praises God’s greatness with a sweep and beauty that exceeds anything the friends have said. The man who is accused of doubting God is the one who describes him best.
observation: Job asks, “Why are times not kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?” (24:1).
He lists the oppressed: the poor driven from the road, orphans taken as a pledge, and laborers who go hungry while they carry the sheaves (24:2-12).
He says, “From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong” (24:12).
Bildad asks, “How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?” (25:4).
He calls man “a maggot” and “a worm” (25:6).
Job answers sarcastically: “How you have helped him who has no power!” (26:2).
He says, “Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering” (26:6).
God “stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing” (26:7).
“Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?” (26:14).
interpretation:
Chapter 24 is a hard chapter to read because it is so honest about injustice. Job does not look away. He describes the poor picking through the leftovers of the rich, children taken as collateral, and the dying crying out in the city. And he says, “God charges no one with wrong.” This is a startling thing for a man of faith to say, but it is true to the way the world looks. Injustice happens, and it seems to go unnoticed. Job is saying what the psalmists say.

It is worth asking what he is asking for. He does not say that God does not exist, and he does not say that God is cruel. He says that the times are not “kept,” that the schedule of judgment is hidden from those who know God. That is a question about timing. And it points forward to a day of judgment, which Job will keep longing for.

Bildad’s speech is a sign that the friends are exhausted. His point in chapter 25 is that no human being is pure before God. That is true, and the New Testament will say it too. But look at what he does with it. He uses it to put Job down, in the cruel language of “maggot” and “worm.” Human weakness is a truth that is supposed to humble us before God. It is not supposed to be used as an insult.

And then Job speaks, and you can hear how much better a theologian he is. He answers Bildad’s short speech with a long, majestic description of God’s power: Sheol is open before him, the earth hangs on nothing, the clouds hold water without bursting, and the pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke. He ends with a humble line that the friends could never say: “These are but the outskirts of his ways.” Even all of this is only the edge of what God is. We hear a whisper. The thunder is beyond us.

This is the proper stance of a creature. Job is not claiming to understand. He is claiming to trust a God who is bigger than his questions.
connection: Psalm 94 asks God, “O LORD, how long shall the wicked exult?” Habakkuk 1:2-4 asks the same question about injustice. Paul says in Romans 11:33 that God’s ways are “unsearchable,” and in 1 Corinthians 13:12 that “now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face.” Revelation 6:10 and 19:2 show God answering the cry for justice.
application:
Make a list of injustices that weigh on you, in your own life, your community, or the world. Do not rush to resolve them. Take them to God as Job does.

Notice whether you tend to use humility as an insult, either toward yourself or toward others.

Then end by praising God for something in creation you cannot explain: the stars, the ocean, or the birth of a child. Remember that these are only the outskirts of his ways.
prayerPrompts: Bring an injustice you see to God.
Thank him that he will one day judge the world in righteousness.
Ask him to make you someone who acts with justice and mercy.
